414.title: Call Him by His names
414.hook: the beautiful names again, in their home verse (7:180)
414.howItsDone: Muslims often begin a du'a with the divine name that fits the request, such as ya Razzaq for provision or ya Ghafur for forgiveness, and many learn the ninety-nine names by heart.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FOURTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: mithaq, the covenant of Alast. Your line was we said yes. Did something feel like remembering? Today, the beautiful names come back, this time in the verse they call home. Day four hundred fourteen.
screen: `MITHAQ — WE SAID YES.`

segments.voice: Back on day two hundred thirty-two, you started a list: the most beautiful names of Allah. The Merciful, the Forgiving, the Provider, the Patient. Maybe you've still got it on a phone note somewhere. Lists of names are lovely to read, and easy to treat like a museum: beautiful things behind glass. But the verse those names come from, in surah seven, doesn't hand them over to be admired. It hands them over to be used. It says what they're for in four words.
screen: `DAY 232, A LIST BEGUN.` → `NAMES BEHIND GLASS?` → `WHAT THEY'RE FOR.`

segments.voice: Verse one-eighty, in Pickthall's words: “Allah's are the fairest names. Invoke Him by them.” In Arabic: wa lillahi al-asma' al-husna, fad'uhu biha. To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call on Him by them. The word for call, ud'u, is the same root as du'a. The names aren't only to know. They're to use, the way you use someone's name to get their attention. So scholars teach matching the name to the need. When you need provision, call on ar-Razzaq, the Provider. When you've done wrong, al-Ghafur, the Forgiving. When you're afraid, as-Salam, Peace. The verse goes on: leave those who distort His names. The verb is yulhiduna, from a root meaning to swerve to one side. A grave in much of the Muslim world has a lahd, a niche dug into the side wall: the same root. To distort the names is to bend them away from what they mean. How many names are there? A hadith in Bukhari says Allah has ninety-nine names, and whoever counts them will enter paradise; scholars explained count as learning them, understanding them, and living by them. But many scholars also held that ninety-nine is not the limit. They cite a du'a reported from the Prophet ﷺ that asks by every name Allah has named Himself, including those He kept hidden with Himself. The list you started is a door, not the whole house. The phrase al-asma' al-husna appears in four places in the Qur'an. This is where the command comes with it.

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Name to yourself one thing you need today, plainly: patience with a child, money for rent, courage for a conversation, rest. Now pick the name that fits it: the Patient, the Provider, the Strong, Peace. If you pray, you can call on Him by that name, quietly, a few times with the breath. If you don't, simply sit with the name and the need side by side. The bell holds the time.

415.title: When it is recited, listen
415.hook: when the Qur'an is recited, listen and be silent (7:204–205)
415.howItsDone: Muslims listen to Qur'an recitation in silence, at home, in the mosque and on the radio; at 7:206, the first prostration verse in the mushaf, many reciters and listeners make a prostration of recitation.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-FIFTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: call Him by His names. Your line was the names are for calling. Which name did you reach for? Today, the last verses of surah seven, and an instruction about your ears. Day four hundred fifteen.
screen: `CALL HIM BY HIS NAMES — THE NAMES ARE FOR CALLING.`

segments.voice: The Prophet ﷺ once asked a companion, Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, to recite the Qur'an to him. Ibn Mas'ud was surprised: recite it to you, when it was revealed to you? The Prophet said he loved to hear it from someone else. So Ibn Mas'ud began reciting surah four, the Women. When he reached a verse about the Day when each community brings a witness, the Prophet said, enough. Ibn Mas'ud looked up and saw his eyes were full of tears. The one who brought the Qur'an, listening to it, in silence.
screen: `RECITE IT TO ME.` → `I LOVE TO HEAR IT FROM ANOTHER.` → `HIS EYES FULL OF TEARS.`

segments.voice: Surah seven ends with three verses about that kind of listening. Verse two-oh-four, in Pickthall's words: “And when the Qur'an is recited, give ear to it and pay heed, that ye may obtain mercy.” Two Arabic verbs. Istami'u: listen closely, lean in with your hearing. And ansitu: be silent, the silence of someone paying attention, not merely not talking. In Mecca, surah forty-one reports, some opponents told each other to make noise whenever the Qur'an was recited, to drown it out. This verse asks for the opposite. Jurists have also debated what it means in congregational prayer. Many Hanafi scholars say the one praying behind an imam should stay silent while he recites, citing this verse. Many Shafi'i scholars hold that each person still recites al-Fatiha quietly, citing a hadith. Both take the verse seriously; they differ on how it applies. Verse two-oh-five continues: remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with awe, below the voice, morning and evening, and don't be among the heedless. And the last verse, two-oh-six, says that those near your Lord are not too proud to worship Him; they glorify Him and prostrate to Him. In the order of the mushaf, this is the first of the verses at which reciters and listeners traditionally bow down in prostration. So al-A'raf, often counted the longest of the Meccan surahs, ends here: ears open, voice low, forehead on the ground. That's the Heights, done.

segments.voice: If you can, play a short recitation of the Qur'an now, any reciter, any surah, at a low volume. If you can't, sit in silence and recall one you've heard, or simply listen to the room. 416.title: Hearts that tremble
416.hook: believers are those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned (8:2)
416.howItsDone: Muslims read 8:2–4 as a portrait of the believer; many scholars cite 8:2 to teach that faith increases and decreases, and recitation is valued for moving the heart.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SIXTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: when it is recited, listen, and surah seven ended in prostration. Your line was listen, be still. Did you hear one recitation through? Today, surah eight, and a heart that moves when it hears. Day four hundred sixteen.
screen: `WHEN IT IS RECITED — LISTEN, BE STILL.`

segments.voice: Surah eight is al-Anfal, the Spoils. It was revealed in Medina after the battle of Badr, in the second year after the emigration, the first major clash between the young Muslim community and the Quraysh of Mecca. And it opens on an awkward note. Right after the battle, the companions are arguing over the spoils: who gets what, who earned more. The very first verse says the spoils belong to Allah and the messenger, so be mindful, and set things right between you. Then the second verse changes the subject completely, from what's in their hands to what's in their hearts.
screen: `AL-ANFAL — THE SPOILS.` → `AFTER BADR, AN ARGUMENT.` → `FROM THE HANDS TO THE HEARTS.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “They only are the (true) believers whose hearts feel fear when Allah is mentioned.” The Arabic verb is wajilat: their hearts tremble, quake, shiver with awe. Pickthall says fear, and the early commentators kept that sense: al-Suddi pictured a man about to do wrong who is told, fear God, and his heart trembles, and he stops. But the word holds awe as well, the shiver you feel standing at the edge of something enormous. The verse goes on: when His verses are recited to them, their faith increases, and they put their trust in their Lord. Then verse three: they establish the prayer and spend from what We've given them. Notice the order. A heart that moves, faith that grows, trust, then prayer and giving. The outward follows the inward. And notice what the verse says faith can do: increase. Many scholars took this verse as evidence that faith isn't a fixed amount; it rises and falls. Here's a puzzle, though. Surah thirteen says that in the remembrance of Allah, hearts find rest. So which is it, trembling or rest? Commentators answered: both. Surah thirty-nine describes it in one breath: skins shiver at the recitation, then skins and hearts soften toward the remembrance of Allah. First the shiver, then the softening. Awe, then peace. A heart that never trembles at anything might be calm, or it might simply be numb. These verses, coming right after a quarrel over spoils, seem to say: if the heart is moved by the right thing, the hands will stop grabbing.

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Think back over the last month: when did your heart actually move? A piece of music, a child's laugh, a verse, a funeral, a sunrise, a stranger's kindness. Find one moment. Remember it in detail until you feel even a faint echo of it now, in your chest. Notice where that feeling lives in your body, and rest there. The bell holds the time.

417.title: You did not throw
417.hook: at Badr, you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw (8:17)
417.tomorrow: Between a man and his heart
417.howItsDone: Muslims often answer praise or good news with alhamdulillah or ma sha' Allah, and teachers cite 8:17 to explain why success is credited to Allah while effort is still expected.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: hearts that tremble. Your line was a heart that trembles. What moved yours? Today, still at Badr, a verse about who gets the credit. Day four hundred seventeen.
screen: `HEARTS THAT TREMBLE — A HEART THAT TREMBLES.`

segments.voice: Watch any award show. The winner gets to the microphone and the first thing they do, almost always, is thank people. My coach, my mom, the team, the crew. Some of it is politeness. But often there's something true in it: they know the trophy has their name on it, and they also know it was never only them. Before the battle of Badr, the sources say the Muslims were badly outnumbered, roughly three to one. Commentators report that as it began, the Prophet ﷺ picked up a handful of pebbles and dust and threw it toward the other army. And afterward, a verse came about that throw.
screen: `THE ACCEPTANCE SPEECH.` → `OUTNUMBERED AT BADR.` → `A HANDFUL OF PEBBLES.`

segments.voice: Verse seventeen begins with the believers: you did not slay them, but Allah slew them. Then it turns to the Prophet, in Pickthall's words: “thou (Muhammad) threwest not when thou didst throw, but Allah threw.” In Arabic it's almost a riddle: wa ma ramayta idh ramayta, wa lakinna Allaha rama. You did not throw, when you threw. The verse doesn't deny that the Prophet's arm moved. It says, you threw, and in the same breath: it wasn't you. Both are true at once. The hand was his; the reaching of that handful, and what came of it, was Allah's. The verse goes on: that He might test the believers with a good test from Him. Even the victory is a test: what will you do with it? Will you say, look at us? Remember yesterday: the surah opened with an argument over the spoils. This verse quietly answers that argument. If the win wasn't only yours, the spoils aren't only yours either. Muslim theologians have spent centuries on this verse, asking how a human act can be both truly yours and truly from God. Different schools gave different answers, and none of them treat the person as a puppet or as the sole cause. The everyday sense of it is simpler, and very old. Effort is real, and it matters. Success is a gift, and it humbles. A common Muslim reflex after any good news, a job, a grade, a recovery, is to say alhamdulillah. In a way, it's this verse, in one word.
screen: `WA MA RAMAYTA — YOU DID NOT THROW.` · `THE HAND WAS HIS; THE REST, ALLAH'S.` · `EVEN VICTORY IS A TEST.` · `EFFORT REAL, SUCCESS A GIFT.` · then, large: `BUT ALLAH THREW.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Think of one thing you're proud of, from this week or this year: something that worked, something you finished, someone you helped. Let yourself feel the effort you put in. It was real. Then widen the picture: the health that let you do it, the people who taught you, the timing you didn't control, the breath in your lungs. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah for it. If not, simply credit what wasn't you. The bell holds the time.
You did not throw. Surah eight, verse seventeen: you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw. The hand is yours; the outcome is His. Today's word.

418.title: Between a man and his heart
418.word: Between a man and his heart
418.hook: Allah comes between a person and his heart (8:24)
418.carry: he is nearer than my heart
418.howItsDone: Many Muslims repeat the Prophet's du'a, ya muqallib al-qulub, thabbit qalbi 'ala dinik (O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm on Your religion), especially in hard or uncertain times.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-EIGHTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: you did not throw. Your line was it wasn't only me. Who did you credit? Today, from the hand to the heart, and a verse that goes closer than anything. Day four hundred eighteen.
screen: `YOU DID NOT THROW — IT WASN'T ONLY ME.`

segments.voice: Some mornings you wake up and you're not sure what you feel about anything. The person you loved last month annoys you. The plan you were sure of looks foolish. And then, a week later, it all flips back. Hearts change. Anyone who's kept a diary knows it: read your own entries from five years ago and you'll meet a stranger. The Arabic word for heart, qalb, comes from a root that means to turn, to flip over. The heart is the thing that turns. Surah eight has a verse about who stands at that turning point.
screen: `A DIARY FROM FIVE YEARS AGO.` → `QALB — THE THING THAT TURNS.` → `WHO STANDS AT THE TURNING?`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-four opens with an invitation: O you who believe, respond to Allah and the messenger when he calls you to what gives you life. Then, in Pickthall's words: “know that Allah cometh in between the man and his own heart,” and that to Him you will be gathered. What does it mean for Allah to come between a person and their heart? Early commentators gave two readings, and both are still taught. One: Allah is closer to you than your own heart. Surah fifty says He is nearer to a person than the vein in their neck. Your heart is the most inward thing you have, and He is nearer still. Two: Allah can turn a heart. He can stand between a person and what their heart wants, or between a person and the faith they assumed they'd always have. So, the verse implies, respond to the call while your heart is open. Don't assume you'll feel the same next year. That second reading explains a du'a the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said often. In Tirmidhi's collection, his wife Umm Salamah says it was the du'a he made most: ya muqallib al-qulub, thabbit qalbi 'ala dinik. O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm on Your religion. When asked why, he said every heart is held between two fingers of the Most Merciful, and He turns it as He wills. That's from a man whose heart his followers trusted completely, asking for steadiness, every day. The heart is not a fortress. It's a door on a hinge, and the verse says who holds the hinge.

segments.voice: Sit, and put a hand on your chest if that feels right. Feel the heartbeat, or just the warmth. Think of one way your heart has turned lately, toward something good or away from it. Notice it without judgment. If you pray, you can say the Prophet's du'a, slowly, in Arabic or English: O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm. If you don't, simply rest with the thought that something nearer than your heart is holding it. The bell holds the time.

419.title: Don't quarrel
419.hook: don't dispute, or you'll lose heart and your strength will go (8:46)
419.howItsDone: Muslim teachers cite 8:46 when calling communities, families and mosque committees to unity, and distinguish respectful scholarly difference (ikhtilaf) from divisive quarreling (tanazu').

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-NINETEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: between a man and his heart. Your line was he is nearer than my heart. Did you notice a turn in your mood? Today, what happens between people when hearts pull in different directions. Day four hundred nineteen.
screen: `BETWEEN A MAN AND HIS HEART — HE IS NEARER THAN MY HEART.`

segments.voice: A sailboat with two people at the helm, each pulling the tiller their own way, goes nowhere. The sail flaps. The boat turns in circles. Everyone's working hard, and all the work cancels out. Families do this. Teams do this. Whole communities do it, over things that look enormous at the time and tiny ten years later. Surah eight remembers a community that had just come through Badr, and was about to learn, a year later at Uhud, what quarreling costs. Its verse forty-six uses the image of wind.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE AT THE TILLER.` → `THE SAIL FLAPS.` → `AN IMAGE OF WIND.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “dispute not one with another lest ye falter and your strength depart from you; but be steadfast!” The verse then adds: Allah is with the steadfast. The Arabic word for dispute is tanaza'u, from a root that means to pull, to snatch: two people tugging the same rope in opposite directions. It's not ordinary disagreement. Companions disagreed all the time, about strategy, about meanings, about rulings, and the Prophet ﷺ often let them. Tanazu' is disagreement turned into a tug-of-war. And the result: fa-tafshalu, you'll lose heart, go slack, fail. And tadhhaba rihukum. Pickthall translates your strength will depart. Literally, your wind will go. In Arabic, a person's wind can mean their power, their momentum, the way we'd say the wind went out of their sails. Some early commentators also took it more literally: the wind of help that blows for a people at their best. Surah three, looking back on Uhud, describes what happened: a group lost heart, disputed over the order they'd been given, and disobeyed, and the day turned. The archers argued over whether to hold their post on the hill, and many left it. So surah eight isn't preaching from nowhere. It's naming a pattern the community would learn the hard way. And the answer it gives is not, never disagree. It's sabr: steadiness. Stay at your post. Hold your tongue when the argument has turned into tugging. Allah is with the steady ones.

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Think of one quarrel you're carrying right now: a group chat argument, a sibling standoff, a cold war with a coworker, a debate you keep replaying in the shower. Ask honestly: is this still a disagreement, or has it become a tug-of-war? What would it cost you to let go of your end of the rope, just this one? Picture letting go. Feel the slack. 420.title: If they incline to peace
420.hook: if they incline to peace, incline to it too, and trust in Allah (8:61)
420.howItsDone: Muslim jurists cite 8:61 for accepting genuine offers of peace and truce, and the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah is taught as its great example; many Muslims also apply it to quarrels between family and friends.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-TWENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: don't quarrel. Your line was quarrels weaken. Did you let go of your end of the rope? A week ends today: the names, the listening, the trembling heart, the throw, the hinge of the heart, the quarrel. Now, peace. Day four hundred twenty.
screen: `DON'T QUARREL — QUARRELS WEAKEN.`

segments.voice: Picture the moment after a long argument when the other person says, quietly, okay, can we stop? It's often not a full apology. Sometimes it's just a cup of tea set down in front of you, or a text with a joke in it. And in that moment, there's a choice. You can say, not until you admit you were wrong. Or you can take the tea. Surah eight was revealed in wartime, between real enemies, about real treaties. And near its end it gives a rule for that exact moment.
screen: `OKAY, CAN WE STOP?` → `A CUP OF TEA SET DOWN.` → `A RULE FOR THAT MOMENT.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “And if they incline to peace, incline thou also to it, and trust in Allah.” The verb is janaha. Its root gives the Arabic word for a wing, janah. To incline, in this sense, is to lean, the way a bird tips its wing as it turns. If they lean toward peace, lean toward it too. The word for peace here is silm, from the same root as salam, and as islam. The next verse anticipates the obvious worry: what if it's a trick? And if they mean to deceive you, Allah is enough for you. In other words, the risk of being fooled is not a reason to refuse an honest-looking offer. Trust in Allah covers it. A few years after Badr, at a place called Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet ﷺ agreed to a treaty with Quraysh whose terms many of his companions found hard to swallow. They were turned back from Mecca that year, and some of the conditions looked one-sided. He accepted. A surah revealed on the way home calls it a clear victory, and in the peace that followed, many more people came to Islam than in the years of fighting. Scholars have debated how this verse sits beside harder verses in the next surah. Some early scholars said those later verses replaced it. Many others, including al-Tabari, held that it still stands, and that peace is to be accepted when it is truly offered. And surah eight, the Spoils, ends a few verses later, with the bonds between believers who stood by each other.
screen: `JANAHA — TO LEAN, LIKE A WING.` · `SILM — PEACE, KIN TO SALAM.` · `IF IT'S A TRICK, ALLAH IS ENOUGH.` · `HUDAYBIYYAH: A CLEAR VICTORY.` · then, large: `INCLINE THOU ALSO TO IT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Think of someone who has recently leaned toward you, even a little, after a rough patch: a message, a favor, a softer tone, an awkward joke. Have you leaned back? Picture yourself accepting it today, without demanding the full apology first. Feel what it's like to tip your wing toward them. And if no one has offered, picture what it would take for you to be the one to lean. The bell holds the time.
If they incline to peace. Surah eight, verse sixty-one: if they lean toward peace, lean toward it too, and trust in Allah. Today's word.
screen: `IF THEY INCLINE TO PEACE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: incline to peace. Today, accept one peace offering, however small, and let it be enough. Surah eight is done. Day four hundred twenty.
